spray-foam-roofing.desc: Spray polyurethane foam roofs with elastomeric coatings for Valley homes and businesses: every benefit, the honest limits and what to ask before you choose.
spray-foam-roofing.h1: Spray foam roofing in the Phoenix Valley
spray-foam-roofing.lead: Of all the roofs we work on, spray polyurethane foam gets the most attention on this site, because few systems answer Arizona's sun, monsoon rain and flat rooflines as well. Here is everything it does, what the coating on top adds, and where the limits are.
spray-foam-roofing.answer: A spray foam roof is closed-cell polyurethane sprayed onto the roof as a liquid, where it expands into one seamless, insulating layer that is then sealed under an elastomeric coating. The foam insulates and sheds water, while the coating blocks UV, reflects heat and can be renewed again and again. Kept coated and inspected, a foam roof can stay in service for decades.

sections.h2: What you're actually buying: two layers with two jobs
sections.body:
A spray foam roof starts as two liquid chemicals that meet at the tip of a spray gun. Within seconds of hitting the roof, the mix swells into rigid, closed-cell polyurethane that grips the surface beneath it. Pass by pass, the crew builds a single continuous layer that insulates the building and sheds water, with no rolls, sheets or overlapping seams across the open roof.

That foam is only half the roof. Polyurethane can't survive direct sunlight, so every foam roof is sealed under an elastomeric coating, a thick, rubbery liquid that cures into a flexible skin. Picture the foam as the roof's insulating core and the coating as its sunscreen and raincoat rolled into one. One without the other isn't a finished roof.

We feature foam more than any other topic on this site because it suits the Valley so well: flat and low-slope roofs, relentless UV, sudden monsoon downpours and rooftops crowded with AC units and coolers. Below we walk through every advantage of the foam, every advantage of the coating over it, and the honest caveats attached to each. If you'd like the basics of foam installation and repair first, our foam roofing overview covers them.

sections.h2: The golden rule: foam never faces the sun alone
sections.body:
If you remember one thing about foam roofs, make it this: bare foam and sunlight don't mix. Ultraviolet light attacks polyurethane. Left uncovered, the surface yellows, then darkens toward rust or brown, turns chalky and crumbly, and slowly wears thinner. Under Arizona sun, that damage starts quickly.

The coating is what stops it. As long as an unbroken layer of coating sits over the foam at the thickness the manufacturer calls for, the foam underneath stays protected and keeps insulating. That's why the rest of this page treats foam and coating as a team, and why most of the long-term care of a foam roof is really care of its coating.

sections.h2: Comfort and energy: what you feel in the rooms below
sections.body:
These four advantages work together to keep summer heat up on the roof instead of inside the house or building.

Foam advantage: a thick, continuous blanket of insulation

Depending on the product, each inch of closed-cell roofing foam is worth roughly R-6 to R-7, and the layer runs edge to edge across the deck with no gaps between boards. That slows heat moving down into the building on summer afternoons and holds warmth in on winter nights. Rooms under the roof tend to keep a steadier temperature, and the air conditioner may not have to work as hard. The size of the change you feel hinges on the insulation already in place, air leakage, how the space is used, the climate and the HVAC equipment.

Foam advantage: fewer air leaks through the roof

Because closed-cell foam is sprayed on and bonds to the deck, it seals gaps and cracks that would otherwise let air slip in and out through the roof assembly. Less leakage can mean fewer drafts, more even comfort and a more efficient HVAC system. The roof is only one piece of the building envelope, though. Leaky windows, doors, walls or ductwork still matter, so the full benefit depends on the whole building.

Coating advantage: sunlight bounced back toward the sky

A white or other highly reflective coating sends much of the sun's energy back off the roof before it can turn into heat. The surface runs cooler, and less heat soaks into the foam and the rooms below. How much it helps comes down to the product's reflectance and emittance ratings, whether the surface stays clean and what insulation lies below.

Foam and coating together: better whole-building energy performance

Stack insulation, air sealing and a reflective surface, and the roof can trim peak cooling demand, slow heat flow through the ceiling and make the spaces under it more comfortable. What it can't do is guarantee a set percentage off your power bill. Every building responds differently, so savings have to be estimated for your building in particular, and we won't quote a number we can't back up.

sections.h2: Keeping water out: seams, details and drainage
sections.body:
Leaks are the reason most people call a roofer. Six of the system's advantages are about keeping water where it belongs.

Foam advantage: one piece, no seams

Most flat roofs that leak do it at a seam, a lap or a fastener. Foam is sprayed in place as one continuous layer. The open roof has no sheet laps at all, water has far fewer joints to find, and few if any fasteners need to punch through. It wraps without a break around penetrations and odd shapes. The caveat: foam is not the whole waterproofing system by itself. It counts on a compatible coating over it to finish the job.

Foam advantage: it surrounds rooftop equipment instead of being cut around it

AC curbs, evaporative coolers, vent stacks, plumbing pipes, conduit and equipment stands are where conventional roofs get cut, patched and lapped, and that's where they tend to leak. Foam is sprayed into and around those shapes, so the details have fewer seams, and it can be built up to tilt water away from equipment. Those spots still need careful flashing and coating work. Foam makes good details easier; it doesn't replace them.

Foam advantage: slope built into the roof itself

Foam doesn't have to go on at one even thickness. By varying the depth from one area to the next, the crew creates fall toward drains and scuppers, fills some low spots and cuts down on ponding where the roof allows it. That has to be laid out from a survey of the roof's high points, low points and drains before spraying starts. And no coating, however good, will cure a serious drainage problem on its own.

Coating advantage: a second waterproof layer

The coating cures into an unbroken film on top of the foam and fills minor pinholes and surface texture, so water has two layers to get through instead of one. It isn't a cure-all. A coating can't dry out wet foam, close major cracks, rescue failed flashing or fix poor drainage. Those get repaired first.

Coating advantage: rain and standing water kept off the foam

Applied properly, the coating keeps monsoon rain and lingering water from reaching the foam. How well it does that comes down to four things: the right thickness, proper surface prep, sound flashing details and a roof that drains.

Coating advantage: it follows every curb, pipe and transition

Applied wet, the coating flows around pipes, vents, curbs and flashing transitions that sheet materials struggle with. Where a detail needs extra strength, reinforcing fabric and compatible sealants are embedded in the coating.

sections.h2: Standing up to heat, storms and wear
sections.body:
Arizona is hard on any roof. These eight advantages are about how the foam and coating hold up to it.

Coating advantage: UV protection, its most important job

Everything else the coating does comes second to this. Foam left unprotected changes color, gets brittle and powdery, and erodes a little more each year. The coating takes the UV punishment so the foam doesn't, which is why an intact coating at full thickness is non-negotiable on an Arizona roof.

Coating advantage: less weathering of the whole system

Sunlight, moisture and the daily swing between scorching afternoons and cooler nights all wear on a roof. The coating takes that abuse first, slowing the deterioration of the foam and everything beneath it.

Coating advantage: it stretches and recovers

Elastomeric coatings flex as the roof grows in the afternoon heat and shrinks back overnight, and they can span hairline cracks in the surface. They can't bridge real structural movement, such as a working expansion joint, unless that spot is specially detailed.

Foam advantage: built for everyday roof stresses

The closed-cell foam made for roofing resists crushing well enough for a roof surface, takes on much less water than open-cell foam does, and keeps its shape and size as temperatures swing. It's tough, not indestructible. It can still be hurt by hard impacts, careless or heavy foot traffic, certain chemicals and sunlight reaching it through worn coating.

Foam advantage: strong resistance to wind uplift

Foam bonds fully to what's beneath it and has very few seams or loose edges, so a strong gust has little to catch and peel back. That matters when monsoon outflow winds hit. The assembly still has to meet the building code's wind requirements for your location and building.

Foam advantage: some resilience against hail and flying debris

The closed-cell structure keeps water from traveling far through the foam if the surface is punctured, and the foam offers a bit of cushion against impacts. Hail can still dent the foam and crack the coating, and wind-driven debris can puncture both. After a hailstorm or a violent monsoon cell, have the roof looked at and get damage repaired quickly.

Coating advantage: a sacrificial wear surface

The coating absorbs the abrasion, minor knocks and weathering that would otherwise grind down the foam. Standard coatings aren't made to be walked on constantly, so walkway pads belong along the routes technicians use to reach equipment.

Coating advantage: some chemical resistance

Coatings can help shield foam from equipment exhaust, airborne contaminants and drips from rooftop units. Resistance varies a lot from product to product, so the coating has to be chosen for what that particular roof is exposed to, such as a kitchen exhaust fan or process equipment.

sections.h2: Fitting the building you already have
sections.body:
Not every roof can take any system. These six advantages explain why foam fits so many buildings that other options don't.

Foam advantage: very little added weight

Foam adds only a small dead load compared with heavier roof systems. That can make it a fit for existing buildings that can't carry more weight, and it may avoid the need for structural reinforcement. Sometimes it can even be applied over the current roof instead of tearing it off, though that decision belongs to a qualified roofer who has evaluated what's already there.

Foam advantage: it bonds to many surfaces

Properly prepared concrete, wood, steel decking and some existing roof surfaces all give SPF something to grab. The bond ties the assembly together and lets foam hug surfaces that aren't flat or even. Whatever the surface, it must be clean, dry, solid and compatible, and some need a primer first for a reliable bond.

Foam advantage: it adapts to awkward roofs

Foam is at home on flat and low-slope roofs, on roofs bristling with penetrations, on irregular outlines with parapets and level changes, on restorations of suitable existing roofs and on roofs that need tapered insulation to drain. An inspection still decides whether your particular roof is a candidate.

Foam advantage: less demolition on the right roof

If the current roof checks out as sound and dry, and the materials are compatible, foam can sometimes be sprayed right over it. That means less tear-off, less debris hauled to the landfill, less noise and mess, and often a shorter job. That option is off the table when the insulation is soaked, moisture is sealed inside, the deck has rotted or deteriorated, or the existing material won't take a bond.

Coating advantage: fire performance, when the assembly is tested

Fire ratings exist for certain foam-and-coating combinations, and they apply only to the exact assembly that was tested and approved. No coating earns a roof a fire rating by itself. Requirements vary with the building and local code, so check the documentation for the specific system on each project.

Coating advantage: a clean, even look

A fresh coat gives the roof a bright, consistent appearance, which matters on roofs you can see from a second story, a neighbor's yard or an office window. Just remember that a good-looking roof isn't proof of a healthy one. Wet foam and failing details can hide under a clean surface, which is why inspections count for more than appearance.

sections.h2: Spending less over the life of the roof
sections.body:
The last nine advantages are about money and effort over the long haul, and the biggest one comes at the end.

Foam advantage: decades of service when it's cared for

Install foam correctly, keep it coated, and have it inspected and maintained, and it can stay in service for decades. The actual lifespan of any one roof hinges on several things: how good the foam is and how thick, how well it bonded, which coating protects it, how much sun and standing water it sees, how much it's walked on, how well it's been repaired and whether the manufacturer's specifications were followed. Plan on renewing the coating a few times over that span while the foam itself remains serviceable.

Foam advantage: repairs are small and local

A puncture, a blister or a gouge doesn't mean replacing a section of roof. The bad spot is cut away, refilled with fresh foam and coated again. Done right, that's far less disruptive than replacement, but the cut has to reach sound, dry foam and the materials have to be compatible, or the leak just shifts to the border of the patch.

Coating advantage: it keeps the insulation dry and working

Foam insulates best when it's dry and intact. Keeping water and UV off the foam means the insulation you paid for keeps doing its job year after year.

Coating advantage: maintenance you can actually plan

Caring for a coated foam roof follows a clear routine: keep the surface clean, keep drains and scuppers open, check penetrations, fix small damage on the spot and recoat when the coating thins. There's very little guesswork about what comes next.

Coating advantage: it stretches the life of the whole system

The foam doesn't get replaced; the coating gets renewed. The cycle is inspection, foam and flashing repairs, surface prep and a new coat at the specified thickness. That cycle keeps working as long as the foam below remains sound and dry.

Coating advantage: renewal can be phased

On a large roof, recoating can sometimes be split into stages to match a budget, starting with the most worn areas. The condition is that no section sits without protection while it waits its turn.

Coating advantage: far less waste at renewal time

When the foam is still sound, a recoat takes the place of a tear-off. That keeps a whole roof's worth of old material out of the landfill.

Foam advantage: a potentially lower cost of ownership

Possible energy savings, fewer full replacements, local repairs, less demolition and recoating instead of re-foaming can all add up over the years. Whether they do for your building depends on the original installation, the maintenance, how often it's recoated and the roof's condition today. We don't publish prices because every roof is different; our Roofing Cost Guide explains what drives the cost.

Coating advantage: a roof you renew instead of replace

This is the advantage that ties the rest together. Plenty of roof systems must be stripped off and hauled away once they're worn out. A foam roof works differently: the surface is renewed while the insulation stays, and a well-kept one can take recoat after recoat over its lifetime. That renewability is the main reason we recommend foam on so many flat roofs.

sections.h2: Choosing the top coat: silicone, acrylic or polyurethane
sections.body:
Three families of elastomeric coating are commonly applied over spray foam. Each family includes many products, and formulation matters, so the table below is a general guide, not a hard rule. The manufacturer's data for the specific product always has the final word.

Here's how we usually think about it. Silicone is our frequent choice on exposed, sun-baked flat roofs, especially where water lingers after a storm. Acrylic is a sensible, water-based option for roofs that shed water quickly and owners watching the budget. Polyurethane, in aliphatic or aromatic versions, earns its place where the roof needs extra toughness, such as regular foot traffic. For many roofs in a hot, sunny climate like ours, white silicone over closed-cell foam is an excellent pairing: it tolerates ponding, resists UV and weather, stays flexible through temperature extremes, reflects heat and is a well-recognized coating for foam. Our page on silicone coating over foam goes deeper, and the elastomeric coatings page covers coatings on other flat roofs.

sections.h2: Where silicone falls short
sections.body: We recommend silicone often, which is exactly why we want you to know its weak spots before you choose it.
bullets: It holds onto dust. Dirt pickup lowers reflectivity over time, and the Valley has no shortage of dust.
Very little sticks to it. Future recoats demand careful cleaning and compatible products, which usually means more silicone.
Some products are soft. Walkways matter wherever people regularly cross the roof.
It doesn't fix what's underneath. Structural problems and poor drainage still have to be corrected.
Installation makes or breaks it. Prep work, reaching full thickness, applying in dry weather and detailing carefully all decide how well it lasts.

sections.h2: Your roof problem, and how foam and coating answer it
sections.body:
Most people don't call us asking for foam. They call about a problem. Here's how the system lines up with the concerns we hear most often from homeowners and building owners.

  • “Our cooling bills are brutal.” Continuous foam insulation slows heat gain, and a reflective coating keeps the surface cooler to begin with.
  • “It keeps leaking.” With no seams in the foam and an unbroken coat on top, the field of the roof loses the joints where many flat-roof leaks begin.
  • “There's so much equipment up there.” Sprayed foam and liquid coating fit the complex shapes around curbs, pipes and stands.
  • “The surface looks tired.” An aging foam roof gets a fresh coat; the foam stays.
  • “Water just sits there.” Tapered foam adds fall so water heads for the drains and scuppers.
  • “We can't afford a tear-off.” A suitable existing roof may be restored instead of removed.
  • “We need something we can keep up with.” Small spot repairs plus a recoat every several years keep it going.
  • “The sun is wrecking it.” The coating takes the UV and weather so the foam doesn't.

sections.h2: A brand-new foam roof or a restored one?
sections.body:
People often lump these together, but they're two different projects with different results.

Installing a new foam system

New foam is sprayed onto a prepared deck, or over an existing roof that checks out sound and dry, and then coated. You gain insulation, a seamless new surface and the chance to correct drainage with tapered foam. It's the right call when you want everything foam offers, or when the current roof is past saving.

Restoring an existing roof with a coating

A sound, dry commercial roof, whether built-up, modified bitumen, single-ply or older foam, can often get a second life from a silicone coating system. The crew cleans it, repairs it, primes it if needed and coats it. It renews the waterproofing and reflectivity, but it adds little insulation and doesn't change the roof's slope.

The right path depends on how much moisture the old roof holds, the deck's condition, drainage, how much insulation you want and budget. On an existing foam roof, renewing the coating is usually the first question to answer; our foam roof recoating page explains how we decide.

sections.h2: What Arizona throws at a foam roof
sections.body:
Our climate is the reason foam and reflective coatings are so common here, and also the reason installation quality and upkeep matter so much.

  • Heat and UV, nearly every day. The desert sun is what wears coatings down and why foam can never be left bare. A bright, reflective top coat pushes back against summer heat gain.
  • Monsoon season, June 15–September 30. Storms arrive fast with heavy rain, gusty outflow winds and blowing debris, testing drainage, flashing and any weak spot in the coating. Foam and coatings won't bond or cure properly on a wet surface, so we plan work around the storm pattern.
  • Dust storms. A haboob can leave a film of dirt across the roof and pack drains and scuppers with silt. That dulls reflectivity and can turn a light rain into ponding, so drains are worth checking after a big one.
  • Hail. It isn't frequent here, but it happens. Hail can dent foam and fracture the coating, so have the roof looked over afterward.
  • Ponding. Flat roofs that hold water wear out their coating fastest in those spots. Tapered foam improves drainage, and silicone handles standing water better than many coatings.

Our storm damage page covers what to do after a severe monsoon storm.

sections.h2: Foam on Valley homes
sections.body:
Spray foam isn't just for warehouses. Plenty of houses across the Valley have flat or low-slope roof areas where foam is often the strongest option.

  • Pueblo Revival and territorial-style homes with flat roofs ringed by parapet walls, where water has to reach a scupper to leave.
  • Flat additions and Arizona rooms tied into a pitched tile or shingle main roof. That tie-in joint needs careful detailing.
  • Patio covers and carports with very little slope, which are prone to ponding.
  • Roofs carrying an AC unit or evaporative cooler, where the foam can wrap the curb and the cooler's drip area.

For a homeowner, that adds up to a seamless roof over living space, extra insulation right where the heat comes in, a cooler surface and a roof you renew rather than replace. If you're in an HOA, ask whether there are rules about roof color or what's visible from the street before work begins. And please keep your own checks to the ground or a window with a view. A slip on a roof isn't worth the risk, and a professional roof inspection is the safer way to see it up close. See residential roofing for everything else we do for homes.

sections.h2: Foam on commercial buildings
sections.body:
Offices, retail centers, warehouses, churches and multi-family buildings in the Valley are mostly flat-roofed and loaded with HVAC equipment. That's where foam's seamless details, tapered drainage, light weight and renewable surface pay off most, and where a restoration over the existing roof can spare tenants the noise and debris of a tear-off.

Our commercial spray foam roofing page is written for owners and property managers, and our broader commercial roofing services page covers everything else we do on commercial roofs.

sections.h2: How long a foam roof lasts, and what to ask about the warranty
sections.body:
According to the Spray Polyurethane Foam Alliance (SPFA), the industry's trade association, foam roofs that get regular inspections and timely recoats can keep working for decades. In real life, the foam usually outlives its first coating. That's expected; the recoat is part of the design, not a sign of failure.

Warranties on foam systems vary widely. Coverage hinges on who made the products, which system was specified, how thick the foam and coating are, who installed it and whether the required maintenance gets done. Manufacturer system warranties come in different lengths depending on the system, but never assume a length or what's covered. When we propose a system, we explain the warranty that comes with it so you know who stands behind what. Before you sign anything, from us or anyone else, get clear answers to these questions:
bullets: Is the warranty from the manufacturer, the installing contractor, or each of them?
Does it pay for labor, materials or both?
Are installation mistakes covered, or only defective products?
Does it exclude damage from ponding water?
What inspections or maintenance must be done, and documented, to keep it valid?
Do future recoats have to be performed by an approved contractor?
If you sell the property, does the coverage pass to the buyer?

sections.h2: The foam system we recommend
sections.body: When a roof is a good candidate for new foam, the system we recommend has five parts, shown in the steps below. Each one leans on the others. Skip any of them and the rest suffer: a skimpy coat lets the sun into good foam, and the best coating made won't save foam that went down over a wet surface.

sections.h2: How we handle a foam project, start to finish
sections.body:
1. Paid inspection. Our roof inspections are a paid service. On a foam roof we check coating wear and thickness, foam condition and adhesion, signs of moisture, the deck, drainage, flashing and rooftop equipment, and we photograph what we find.
  2. A straight recommendation. We explain whether repairs, a recoat, a restoration, new foam or another system entirely makes the most sense, and why.
  3. Written estimate. You get a written estimate describing the scope of work. Financing is available; ask about it during the estimate.
  4. Scheduling around the weather. Spraying and coating wait for dry surfaces and the right temperatures. We work around monsoon storms and arrange roof access with you, your HOA or your tenants.
  5. Prep and installation. The surface is cleaned and repaired, foam and coating go on at the thicknesses specified, and every penetration, drain and flashing gets detailed.
  6. Walkthrough and care plan. We go over the completed roof together and suggest a schedule for inspections and the next recoat.

faqs: Is a spray foam roof considered a cool roof?

A foam roof finished with a bright white, reflective coating works as a cool roof, since most of the sunlight hitting it bounces away rather than turning into heat. Unlike a coating alone, it also adds a continuous layer of insulation underneath. Bear in mind that dust gradually dulls the surface, and a cleaner roof stays cooler.
Why does Integrity Roofing feature spray foam more than other flat roof systems?

Foam fits the conditions Valley roofs face: intense UV, flat and low-slope rooflines, crowded rooftop equipment and sudden monsoon rain. It insulates, has no field seams, can be shaped for drainage and renews with a recoat instead of a tear-off. It isn't right for every roof, and an inspection decides that.
Can foam be sprayed on just one flat section of my house?

Yes. Many homes have foam only on a flat addition, Arizona room or patio cover while the main roof is tile or shingle. The important part is the joint where the flat section meets the pitched roof, which needs careful flashing so water from the main roof doesn't get behind the foam.
Is spray foam a good fit for a pueblo-style home with parapet walls?

Often it is. Foam can run up the inside of parapet walls, wrap around scuppers and be tapered so water moves toward the exits instead of collecting along the walls. Parapet caps and stucco still need to be in good shape, because water that gets in at the top of a wall can bypass the roof entirely.
Does closed-cell foam soak up water if the coating gets punctured?

Closed-cell foam takes on much less water than the open-cell kind, and its sealed cells limit how far water travels from a puncture. It isn't immune, though. Water left to work into a damaged spot can wet the surrounding foam, so punctures should be repaired promptly.
Which layer of a foam roof actually keeps the rain out?

Both layers share the job. The foam is a seamless, water-shedding body, and the coating adds a continuous waterproof film while protecting the foam from UV. If the coating wears through, the foam is exposed to sun and water, which is why recoating on schedule matters.
Why does roof weight matter when choosing a flat roof system?

Every roof system adds dead load that the structure has to carry. Some older buildings, patio covers and additions weren't built with much extra capacity, which limits the heavier options. Foam adds very little weight, which is one reason it fits so many existing structures.
Can foam go over an old tar and gravel roof?

Sometimes. Loose gravel generally has to be removed and the surface cleaned, and the old roof must be dry, sound and compatible with foam. If moisture is trapped in the old layers or the deck is damaged, that material has to come off first.
How is a foam roof different from a modified bitumen roof?

Modified bitumen is installed in rolls with overlapping seams, while foam is sprayed as one seamless layer that also adds insulation and can be tapered for drainage. Modified bitumen handles foot traffic well and is common on commercial roofs. Foam is renewed with a recoat rather than new sheets, so which one wins depends on the building and how the roof gets used.
What details should I compare between two foam roof proposals?

Compare the foam thickness, whether tapering for drainage is included, the coating type and specified thickness, how wet or damaged areas will be handled and how penetrations and walkways will be detailed. Also compare whose warranty applies and what maintenance it requires. A lower number that leaves out prep or thickness isn't the same roof.
Is there a charge for a foam roof inspection?

Yes. Roof inspections are a paid service at Integrity Roofing. On a foam roof we check coating thickness and wear, foam condition, moisture, drainage, flashing and equipment, then explain what we found and what we recommend.
What is the most common reason foam roofs fail early?

Letting the coating wear through is the biggest one. Once UV reaches bare foam, the surface breaks down and water follows. Thin original coatings, ponding that goes unaddressed and poorly detailed penetrations are the other usual causes.
Can a foam roof warranty transfer to the next owner?

Some can and some can't, and transfers sometimes require notice, an inspection or a fee set by the warranty issuer. Read the actual warranty document and ask before you buy or sell. When we propose a system, we explain the warranty that comes with it, including whether it transfers.
Will a foam roof help with a hot Arizona room or patio enclosure?

It can help, because many of these rooms sit under a thin, poorly insulated flat roof. Foam adds continuous insulation and a reflective surface right over the space. Single-pane windows and walls also let heat in, so results depend on the whole room.
Does a foam roof need different attention in summer than in winter?

Summer brings the most UV and the monsoon, so drains, scuppers and the coating deserve a close look before and after storm season. Winter is milder on the roof, but dew and occasional rain matter for scheduling coating work. Inspections before and after monsoon season cover both.

silicone-coating-over-foam.title: Silicone Coating Over Spray Foam Roofs | Integrity Roofing
silicone-coating-over-foam.desc: How white silicone compares with acrylic and polyurethane over spray foam: ponding, dust and reflectivity, recoat rules, mil thickness, prep and exceptions.
silicone-coating-over-foam.h1: Silicone coating over spray foam: when it's the right top coat
silicone-coating-over-foam.lead: The coating is the part of a foam roof that faces the weather every day, so choosing it is one of the biggest decisions in the whole system. Here's how silicone stacks up against acrylic and polyurethane, and when we'd pick something else.
silicone-coating-over-foam.answer: On Arizona flat roofs, white silicone is often the best top coat for spray foam: it resists UV, usually copes well with standing water and reflects heat when clean. The trade-offs are that it collects dirt, some products are soft, and later recoats generally have to be silicone as well. Whether it suits your roof comes down to drainage, how much the roof is walked on and what coating is up there now.
silicone-coating-over-foam.card_text: Silicone vs acrylic vs polyurethane over foam.
silicone-coating-over-foam.service_type: Silicone elastomeric coating over spray polyurethane foam

sections.h2: Why silicone is our usual pick on Valley foam roofs
sections.body:
Spray foam is the insulating body of the roof, and the coating over it is the weathering surface. That surface takes direct sun, monsoon rain, dust, heat and foot traffic, and its first job is to keep UV off the foam. Of the coatings commonly used over foam, white silicone is the one we recommend most often in the Valley.

The reasons line up neatly with our climate:

  • It holds up where water sits. Even a well-drained flat roof may hold some water after a hard storm, and silicone generally handles that better than other common coatings.
  • It shrugs off UV and weather. Silicone breaks down slowly under intense sun, which Valley roofs get most of the year.
  • It stays flexible at both extremes. It keeps moving with the roof through scorching afternoons and cool nights.
  • It reflects heat. Clean and white, silicone throws much of the sun's energy back off the roof.
  • It's an established choice for foam. Silicone is a well-recognized protective coating for SPF systems.

That's the case for it. The rest of this page covers the other options and the situations where silicone is the wrong call.

sections.h2: Silicone, acrylic and polyurethane in more depth
sections.body:
Each of these coating families includes many products from many manufacturers, and the specific formulation matters as much as the family. Treat what follows as general guidance.

Silicone: the ponding-tolerant workhorse

Silicone's strengths are UV resistance, generally excellent tolerance of ponding water and excellent reflectivity when it's new and white. It cleans up with solvents rather than water. Its weaknesses are that it tends to collect dirt, that abrasion resistance varies and some products are fairly soft, and that recoating it later requires compatible preparation and materials, often silicone over silicone. It's a good fit for exposed roofs, especially where ponding is a concern.

Acrylic: water-based and budget-friendly

Acrylic coatings are water-based, so tools and spills clean up with water, and they offer generally good UV resistance and excellent reflectivity when new and white. Their main limitation is water that sits: under prolonged ponding, many acrylics soften and wear faster. They make the most sense on roofs with good drainage where budget is a priority, and they're widely used on foam roofs that shed water well.

Polyurethane: built for abuse

There are two main polyurethane types, aliphatic and aromatic, and the specific formulation drives how any one product behaves. Certain formulations stand up to scuffing and abrasion exceptionally well, which makes them useful on roofs that need extra durability or get walked on regularly. On some systems they appear as a base coat or in traffic areas, with a different top coat elsewhere.

sections.h2: Ponding: tolerance is not a drainage plan
sections.body:
Ponding is water still standing on the roof a day or two after the rain stops. During monsoon season it's one of the fastest ways to wear out a coating: the water holds dirt against the surface, keeps the coating wet for days and adds weight to the structure.

Silicone's tolerance for standing water is a real advantage, and it's one of the main reasons we use it on flat roofs that can't be made to drain perfectly. But tolerating ponding isn't the same as solving it. Water that keeps returning to the same low spot is still a sign of a drainage problem, and it still finds any weakness at a seam, curb or flashing.

Where we can, we fix the cause. On a foam roof that might mean adding foam to build slope toward a drain or scupper, opening up a clogged drain or scupper after a dust storm, or building a small cricket behind equipment that traps water. Also check any warranty for a ponding exclusion before counting on a coating to handle standing water by itself.

sections.h2: Dust, dirt pickup and how bright the roof stays
sections.body:
On the day it's applied, a white silicone roof is about as reflective as a roof gets. That brightness is what keeps the surface cooler and cuts the heat moving into the building. Silicone has a habit of holding onto dust, though, and Valley roofs collect plenty of it, especially after a haboob rolls through.

A dusty, darker surface bounces back less sunlight and soaks up more heat. Here's what that means in practice:

  • Expect some loss of brightness over the first few years as dust works into the surface.
  • Cleaning can bring back some reflectivity, but only use methods the coating manufacturer approves, and leave the roof work to professionals.
  • Dark streaks or rings usually mark where water ponds and leaves dirt behind as it dries.
  • A dirty surface also has to be thoroughly cleaned before any recoat, or the new coating won't bond.
  • Real-world energy gains hinge on the product's reflectance and emittance ratings, its cleanliness and the insulation beneath.

sections.h2: Recoating a silicone roof: what will and won't stick
sections.body:
This is the part of choosing silicone that people most often wish they'd known sooner. Silicone is very hard for other materials to bond to. After silicone goes on a roof, the next coat is generally silicone as well, applied after careful cleaning and whatever preparation the manufacturer specifies. Some systems call for a primer or an adhesion test first.

That has practical effects down the road:

  • Know what's on the roof. Before any recoat, the existing coating has to be identified, because the wrong product over it can peel.
  • The direction matters. Silicone can often be applied over a well-prepared acrylic surface, but putting most other coatings over silicone is a different story.
  • Repairs follow the same rule. Sealants, patching compounds and fabric used on a silicone roof must be compatible with silicone.
  • Records save trouble. Writing down the product, the color and the date of each coating makes the next recoat far simpler.

sections.h2: Thickness and prep: where coatings succeed or fail
sections.body:
Two coatings from the same bucket can perform very differently depending on what's underneath and how much goes on. These are the factors that decide it.

Getting the surface ready

The surface has to be clean, dry and sound. On a recoat, dust, loose coating and contaminants come off first. Blisters, punctures, damaged foam and failed flashing get fixed, and wet foam is removed and refilled. Primer is used where the product or surface calls for it.

Building enough mils

Each coating system calls for a set thickness in mils. That build is what gives the product its UV protection and its designed service life. A coat stretched thin to cover more area wears through early. We follow the manufacturer's thickness requirement, often building it up over multiple passes, and measure along the way. In traffic areas, granules may be scattered into the wet coating for extra wear resistance.

Waiting for the right weather

Coatings need dry surfaces and suitable temperatures to cure. We plan around monsoon storms, June 15–September 30, and watch for heavy dew on cool nights, which can affect curing.

sections.h2: When we'd steer you away from silicone
sections.body:
Silicone is our frequent choice, not our only one. We'll recommend something else, or more than a coating, when:

  • The roof sees heavy foot traffic. A tougher polyurethane, or silicone with well-placed walkway pads, may serve better.
  • Water runs off quickly and the budget is tight. A quality acrylic is a reasonable option where water doesn't sit.
  • The existing coating rules it out, or keeping future recoat options open matters to you.
  • The roof is exposed to specific chemicals, such as kitchen exhaust or process equipment, that call for a product chosen for that exposure.
  • The underlying issue is the structure or the drainage. A coating can't correct a sagging deck, soaked insulation or a roof built to hold water.
  • The roof is too far gone. Saturated foam or a damaged deck has to be repaired or replaced before any coating goes on.

Whichever coating you choose, the workmanship matters more than the brand on the pail. Prep, mil thickness, dry conditions and penetration details are what decide how it holds up.

faqs: Why do roofers recommend white silicone so often in Arizona?

White silicone resists UV, usually copes with the water that collects on flat roofs after monsoon storms and, when clean, reflects much of the sun's heat. It also stays flexible through big daily temperature swings. Those strengths match the Valley's climate closely.
If my foam roof has acrylic now, can the next coat be silicone?

Often, yes. Silicone can usually be applied over an acrylic surface that has been cleaned, repaired and prepared the way the manufacturer specifies, sometimes with a primer. Going from silicone back to acrylic is much harder, so it's worth deciding with the long term in mind.
How can you tell what coating is already on my roof?

Records from the last coating job are the easiest answer. Without them, a roofer looks at the surface and may do a small adhesion test with the planned product to confirm compatibility before committing to a recoat.
Does silicone lose its reflectivity over time?

Some, yes. Silicone tends to hold dust, and the dirt dulls the surface so it reflects less heat than when it was new. Manufacturer-approved cleaning can restore part of it, and a clean surface is required before a recoat anyway.
Is silicone harder to repair than acrylic?

Repairs on silicone are very doable, but they require silicone-compatible materials and a clean surface, since most other sealants won't bond to it. Acrylic is more forgiving about what goes over it. Either way, the repair has to reach sound foam to last.
Is acrylic ever the smarter choice over foam?

Yes. On a foam roof that drains well, with little or no ponding, a quality acrylic is a reflective, water-based option that often fits a tighter budget. It also keeps future recoat choices more open than silicone does.
What is the difference between aliphatic and aromatic polyurethane coatings?

Aliphatic polyurethanes are formulated to hold up in sunlight and keep their color, so they can serve as a top coat. Aromatic types are generally less stable in sunlight, so they commonly serve as a base layer beneath a different top coat. Exact performance depends on the product.
How many coats of silicone go on a foam roof?

It depends on the system and the thickness the manufacturer specifies. On many roofs it's built up over several passes so the full thickness is reached evenly. What matters is the finished thickness, not the number of passes.
Why do crews check coating thickness during application?

Thickness is what gives a coating its protection and service life, and it's easy to spread a coat too thin over a large roof. Checking as the work goes lets the crew add coating where it's light before it cures, instead of finding thin spots years later.

foam-roof-recoating.title: Foam Roof Recoating in Gilbert & Phoenix | Integrity Roofing
foam-roof-recoating.desc: When to recoat a spray foam roof, what we check first, how repair-then-recoat works, what wet foam and deck damage mean, and how recoats can be staged.
foam-roof-recoating.h1: Foam roof recoating: renew the surface, keep the foam
foam-roof-recoating.lead: A foam roof is designed to have its coating renewed, not to be torn off when the surface wears. Catching that moment at the right time is what keeps the job simple and the roof going for decades.
foam-roof-recoating.answer: Recoating a foam roof means cleaning it, cutting out and replacing any wet or damaged foam, repairing flashing and details, then applying a new coating to the specified thickness. It's time to recoat when the coating looks chalky or thin, or when tan, orange or brown foam starts showing. A recoat only works when the foam underneath is sound and dry.
foam-roof-recoating.card_text: Warning signs, repairs and recoating for foam roofs.
foam-roof-recoating.service_type: Spray foam roof repair and recoating

sections.h2: What a recoat is, and what it isn't
sections.body:
On a spray foam roof, the coating is the part that wears. It absorbs sunlight, rain, dust and footsteps on the foam's behalf, and over the years it slowly chalks, thins and weathers away. A recoat replaces that worn protection with a fresh layer, while the insulating foam stays where it is.

A recoat isn't a paint job, and it isn't a way to hide problems. A new coating over wet foam, open blisters or failed flashing traps the damage underneath and fails early. That's why every recoat we do starts with an inspection and repairs, and why the coating is the last step, not the first.

A recoat every 5–10 years is common, with the interval set by the coating type, its original thickness, how much sun and standing water it sees and how often it's walked on. Your roof's actual condition matters more than the calendar.

sections.h2: Warning signs you can spot from the ground
sections.body: You don't need to climb up to know something's changing. From the yard, a second-story window or a neighbor's vantage point, watch for these:
bullets: A dull, chalky or patchy surface where the coating used to look bright and even
Yellow, tan, orange or brown areas, which usually mean bare foam is facing the sun
Rough, eroded texture where the bumpy foam surface is showing through the coating
Raised bubbles or blisters, which can mean trapped moisture or lost adhesion
Small pits or holes, often from birds pecking at the surface
Dark rings or dirt stains that mark where water ponds after storms
Worn paths around AC units, coolers and roof hatches
Ceiling stains or drips inside, which mean water has already found a way in

sections.h2: Why waiting makes the job bigger
sections.body:
The cost and effort of a recoat depend mostly on what's under the old coating when the work starts. If the coating is thin but still covering the foam, the job is mostly cleaning, minor repairs and a new coat.

Once the coating wears through, the clock speeds up. UV breaks down the exposed foam, turning the top layer brittle and powdery, and that weathered foam has to be ground or cut away before new coating will hold. Holes and blisters left open let water into the foam, and wet foam has to be removed and replaced. Each of those adds labor and material that a timely recoat would have avoided.

So the best time to recoat is a little before you think you need to, while the foam is still protected. Our Roofing Cost Guide explains the factors that affect what a recoat involves.

sections.h2: What our inspection looks at before we recommend anything
sections.body:
Our roof inspections are a paid service, and on a foam roof they're the foundation of every recommendation. We want to know what's under the surface before suggesting a recoat, a repair or something bigger. A typical foam roof inspection covers:

  • Coating thickness and wear, including thin spots and any exposed foam
  • The existing coating type, since the new coating has to be compatible, especially over silicone
  • Foam condition: blisters, soft spots, erosion, cracks and adhesion
  • Moisture, because wet foam or wet insulation must be found and removed, never coated over
  • Drainage: drains, scuppers and the areas where water ponds
  • Flashing and penetrations at parapets, curbs, pipes, vents and equipment
  • Signs of deck trouble, such as sagging areas or interior leaks

We photograph what we find and explain whether the roof is ready for a recoat, needs repairs first or needs a different approach. If you'd like to know more about the inspection itself, see roof inspections.

sections.h2: The repair-then-recoat process
sections.body:
When a roof checks out as a good candidate, the recoat follows the sequence in the steps below. Every step exists to make sure the new coating bonds to clean, dry, sound foam and that the weak spots are fixed before they're covered.

Coatings need dry surfaces to cure, so we schedule recoats for dry stretches and plan around monsoon storms, June 15–September 30.

sections.h2: Wet foam and damaged decks: when a recoat isn't enough
sections.body:
Moisture is the dividing line between a straightforward recoat and a bigger project. A few small wet patches are routine: they're cut back to dry, sound foam and refilled during the repair stage.

Widespread moisture is different. Saturated foam or insulation loses much of its insulating value, won't hold a coating and keeps feeding water into the roof. Coating over it only seals the problem in. When moisture runs through large areas, the wet material has to come out, and sometimes the whole system does.

The deck matters too. Rotted wood, a corroded deck or sagging between supports has to be repaired before anything new goes on top, and that means removing the roofing above the damage. Other signs that removal may be needed include foam that has lost its bond over large areas, materials that aren't compatible with foam or the planned coating, and a building that can't carry any added layers.

sections.h2: Recoat, re-foam or replace?
sections.body:
Most foam roofs fall into one of three paths. We'll tell you which one yours is on, including when it doesn't need the bigger job.

Recoat

The foam is sound and dry, and the coating is worn. Clean, make local repairs, recoat. This is the most common and least disruptive option.

Re-foam and recoat

The foam is mostly sound but has weathered, eroded or developed low spots. A new layer of foam goes over the prepared surface, sometimes tapered to improve drainage, and then the coating. You gain back thickness and insulation without a tear-off.

Replace

Moisture runs through much of the roof, the deck has been damaged, or big sections of foam no longer bond. The affected roofing comes off, the deck is repaired and a new system goes on. Our roof replacement page covers what that involves.

sections.h2: A maintenance calendar for Valley foam roofs
sections.body:
Timing your inspections around the seasons catches most problems while they're still small.

  • Spring, before the heat and storms: look at coating wear, clean out drains and scuppers, and close up any openings before the storms.
  • After monsoon season ends, around October: look for storm damage, hail marks, debris and ponding, and clean out drains.
  • After any haboob, hailstorm or severe storm: a quick check for punctures, clogged drains and coating damage.
  • When the coating is getting thin: plan the recoat for a dry, mild stretch rather than waiting for bare foam.
  • Ongoing: keep debris off the roof, keep technicians on walkway pads and get small damage repaired promptly.

Plan the recoat a season or two ahead so it can be scheduled in good weather instead of rushed after a leak.

sections.h2: Renewing a large roof in stages
sections.body:
Recoating a big roof all at once isn't always possible within one year's budget. In many cases it can be split into phases. The most urgent areas go first: anywhere foam is exposed, ponding zones that have worn through and traffic paths around equipment. The remaining sections follow on a planned schedule.

One rule doesn't bend: every section stays protected while it waits its turn. Exposed foam gets repaired and coated right away, even if the full recoat of that section comes later. A written plan that maps which sections were done and when keeps everyone on the same page, which matters even more when building managers or HOA boards change.

sections.h2: Keep a roof history file
sections.body: A simple folder makes every future recoat easier. Keep the installation date, the foam and coating products used, the coating color, each recoat date and product, inspection reports and photos, and any repairs with their locations. That record tells the next roofer what coating is on the roof, which matters for compatibility, and it's often needed to keep a warranty in force.

sections.h2: Schedule a foam roof inspection
sections.body:
Integrity Roofing is a family-owned Valley contractor in business since 1993, and foam roof repairs and recoats are part of our regular work for homes and commercial buildings. Call 602-548-3770 between 7 am and 5 pm, Monday to Friday, or email office.integrityroofing@gmail.com to schedule a paid inspection. You'll get a written estimate, and financing is available. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

For the full overview of foam roofs, see spray foam roofing.

steps: Clean the surface
Dust, dirt and debris come off so the new coating can bond. Valley roofs collect a lot of dust, so this step is never skipped.
Cut out wet and damaged foam
Wet, weathered or loose foam is removed back to sound, dry material. Stopping short only relocates the problem to the border of the repair.
Re-foam and seal
Fresh foam fills the cut-outs. Blisters get fixed, bird pecks and punctures are closed up, and low areas may be built higher.
Repair flashing and details
Curbs, pipes, parapet transitions, drains and scuppers get repairs, plus compatible fabric or sealant wherever a detail needs reinforcing.
Prime where required
Some surfaces and coatings need a primer for a reliable bond, especially when changing coating types.
Coat to the specified thickness
Fresh coating is built up to the thickness the manufacturer calls for, often in several passes, and traffic areas get granules or walkway pads.
Walk the finished roof
We check the details, review the work with you and recommend when the next inspection should happen.
faqs: Is there a limit to how many times a foam roof can be recoated?

Not a set number. Renewing the coating again and again is how a foam roof is designed to work. While the foam stays sound and dry and each new coat is compatible with the last, the roof can keep being renewed.
Does the old coating have to be removed before a recoat?
Usually not all of it. Coating that is still well bonded is cleaned and prepared, while loose, peeling or failed coating is removed. The new coating has to be compatible with what remains.
How is a foam roof cleaned before a recoat?

The surface is cleaned to remove dust, dirt and loose material using methods that suit the existing coating and the new product. Drains and scuppers are cleared too. A roof that looks clean from the ground can still carry a film of dust that would keep a new coating from bonding.
Can I stay in my home normally during a foam roof recoat?

In most cases, yes. Recoats are done from the roof, though you may notice some noise and coating odor, and we may ask you to keep windows near the work closed and turn off an evaporative cooler or fresh-air intake while we're working near it. We'll go over what to expect before we start.
How do you find wet foam if the surface looks fine?

Moisture often hides under an intact-looking coating. We look for soft spots, blisters and interior leak history, and we may take small core samples or use moisture-detection tools in suspect areas. Any wet foam found is cut out and replaced before recoating.
What does a soft spot on a foam roof usually mean?

A soft or spongy area often means the foam is wet, has lost its bond to the surface below or has been damaged by traffic. It should be opened up and evaluated. Depending on the cause, the area is cut out, re-foamed and recoated, or the deck beneath is checked further.
Is it too late to recoat if I can already see brown foam?

Usually not, but the job gets bigger. Weathered foam has to be removed back to sound material, and sometimes a new layer of foam is added before coating. The longer bare foam sits in the sun and rain, the more of it has to be replaced.
Is it better to schedule a recoat ahead of the monsoon or after it?

Ideally before, so the roof goes into the storms with full protection, and during a dry stretch so the coating can cure. If the roof is already showing bare foam in summer, repairing and sealing those areas shouldn't wait for fall.
Will a recoat fix a leak I already have?

Only if the leak's cause is repaired first. Leaks often come from flashing, a curb, a blister or wet foam, and those spots are fixed before the new coating goes on. A coating alone over an active leak usually just moves the problem.

commercial-spray-foam-roofing.title: Commercial Spray Foam Roofing, Phoenix AZ | Integrity Roofing
commercial-spray-foam-roofing.desc: Spray foam roofing for Valley commercial buildings: sealing HVAC curbs, fixing drainage, cutting heat gain, restoring without tear-off and planned upkeep.
commercial-spray-foam-roofing.h1: Commercial spray foam roofing for owners and property managers
commercial-spray-foam-roofing.lead: Most commercial roofs in the Valley are flat, crowded with equipment and baking in the sun. Spray foam with a reflective coating answers each of those problems, and on the right building it can be installed or renewed without tearing off the existing roof.
commercial-spray-foam-roofing.answer: Commercial spray foam roofing is a seamless, insulating roof sprayed onto a prepared deck or a sound existing roof and finished with a reflective elastomeric coating. It wraps tightly around HVAC curbs and penetrations, can be built up to fix drainage and gets renewed with periodic recoats. A paid inspection with moisture checks tells you whether your building qualifies.
commercial-spray-foam-roofing.card_text: Foam roofing for offices, retail and multi-family buildings.

sections.h2: Why foam fits so many commercial roofs in the Valley
sections.body:
Offices, retail centers, warehouses, churches, medical buildings and multi-family properties here share a roof profile: flat or low-slope, lined with parapets, studded with HVAC units and sitting under some of the most intense sun anywhere in the country. Spray polyurethane foam topped with an elastomeric coating suits that profile well.

For an owner or manager, the appeal comes down to a few practical points. Foam is one seamless layer, so the field of the roof has no seams to open up. It adds insulation over the whole deck. It's light enough to go on many existing buildings without structural work. It can be shaped to move water. And when the surface wears, it's recoated rather than torn off, which keeps the roof in the maintenance budget instead of the capital budget more often.

It isn't the answer for every building, and we'll say so when it isn't. Our main spray foam roofing page walks through every advantage and limit in detail; this page focuses on what matters for commercial property.

sections.h2: HVAC curbs, penetrations and the leaks they cause
sections.body:
Ask any property manager where their roof leaks and the answer is usually near equipment. Rooftop units, exhaust fans, gas lines, condensate lines, conduit, plumbing vents and equipment supports all break through or sit on the roof, and on sheet-type systems each one means cutting, lapping and sealing.

Foam goes on as a liquid and expands into and around those shapes, so the details end up with far fewer seams. It can also be built up around a curb to direct water away from it. The coating follows the same contours, with reinforcing fabric and compatible sealant added at the details that need extra strength.

Details still demand skill. Curb heights, flashing, the coating thickness at each penetration and the condition of the equipment's own housing all matter. And service traffic is one of the biggest threats to a commercial foam roof, so we recommend walkway pads along the routes HVAC technicians take and ask that contractors avoid dragging tools or setting sharp equipment on the coating.

sections.h2: Drainage on large flat roofs
sections.body:
On a big flat roof, small sags add up. Water left behind by a monsoon cell wears out the coating faster, traps dirt and debris, puts extra weight on the structure and finds every weak spot. Drains and scuppers clogged with silt after a dust storm make it worse.

Foam gives you a tool most systems don't: its depth can vary across the roof, creating fall toward drains and scuppers and filling some low areas. That plan comes from surveying the roof before any spraying, and it suits many roofs but not all. Roof drains may also need attention so the new surface still flows into them properly. If some ponding can't be designed away, silicone usually handles lingering water better than most other coatings. See silicone coating over foam for how we choose coatings.

sections.h2: Cooling loads and top-floor comfort
sections.body:
A commercial roof is a large surface soaking up heat all day. Each inch of closed-cell foam provides around R-6 to R-7, depending on the product, in one continuous layer over the deck, and it cuts the air that leaks through the roof assembly. A white reflective coating on top sends much of the sun's energy back off the roof before it becomes heat.

Combined, they can trim peak cooling loads, slow heat flow indoors and make top-floor suites, upper apartments and warehouse floors more comfortable. Real results vary with the insulation already there, how the building is used, air leakage elsewhere in the envelope, the HVAC equipment and how well the coating is kept clean. Energy savings need to be estimated for your specific building, and we don't promise a fixed percentage.

sections.h2: Keeping tenants, customers and operations running
sections.body:
On a commercial job, the roof is only part of the project. The rest is the people under it. Foam and coating projects can be easier on a building than a full tear-off: less demolition, fewer dumpsters, less debris near entrances and often a shorter schedule.

Spraying does bring its own coordination needs, and we plan them with you before work starts:

  • Air intakes. Rooftop units and fresh-air intakes near the work may need to be shut down or protected so odor and overspray don't get drawn inside.
  • Wind. Foam is sprayed only when wind conditions allow, which protects cars, neighboring buildings and the work itself.
  • Access and staging. We confirm how we'll reach the roof and where equipment will sit so entrances, parking and deliveries keep moving.
  • Notice. Letting tenants know the schedule ahead of time prevents most complaints.
  • Weather. Coatings need dry weather, so monsoon storms shape the calendar and we'll keep you posted if dates move.

sections.h2: Restoring the roof you have instead of tearing it off
sections.body:
If your building already has a built-up, modified bitumen, single-ply or older foam roof, it may not need to come off. A roof that is still sound and dry can often be restored in one of two ways.

Coating restoration

We clean and repair the existing roof, prime it where required and coat it, usually with silicone. You get a renewed waterproof, reflective surface with relatively little disruption. It doesn't add meaningful insulation or change the roof's slope.

New foam over the existing roof

After prep, closed-cell foam goes directly over the old roof and is then coated. You get added insulation, a seamless new surface and the chance to correct drainage, without the demolition.

Neither option works when the insulation is soaked, moisture is sealed inside, the deck has deteriorated or the materials aren't compatible. That's why we check for moisture before recommending either. Our foam roof recoating page explains how we tell a restorable roof from one that has to come off.

sections.h2: Building a maintenance program
sections.body:
Foam roofs earn their long service life through maintenance, and commercial roofs do best on a written program rather than reacting to leak calls. The table on this page lays out what a typical program includes and why each piece matters.

A program also gives you something a reactive approach can't: a paper trail. Inspection reports, photos, repair records and recoat dates help with budgeting, support warranty requirements and give the next manager or buyer a clear picture of the roof. On larger roofs, recoats can be phased section by section, provided nothing is left exposed in the meantime.

sections.h2: Warranty questions owners and managers should ask
sections.body: On a commercial roof, warranty details matter more than the headline number of years. The terms turn on the product maker, the specified system, foam and coating thickness, who did the installation and whether required maintenance was kept up. When we propose a system, we explain the warranty that comes with it. Whoever you work with, get written answers to these:
bullets: Which company stands behind the roof, the product maker, the roofing contractor or the two together?
Are both labor and materials covered if something fails?
Does coverage include workmanship problems, not just product defects?
Is damage from ponding water excluded?
What inspection and maintenance records must we keep for the warranty to stay in force?
Do future recoats have to be done by an approved applicator?
Does the coverage transfer if the building is sold?

sections.h2: Planning the roof budget over the building's life
sections.body:
Foam can be a cost-effective commercial roof over time because of possible energy savings, local repairs, less demolition and recoats in place of replacement. Whether it works out that way depends on the initial installation, the maintenance program and the roof's starting condition.

For capital planning, the useful approach is to treat the roof as a cycle: installation or restoration, annual inspections and small repairs, then a recoat when the coating thins. Knowing roughly when each recoat is due lets you budget for it years ahead. We don't publish prices because every roof is different; the Roofing Cost Guide explains what drives cost.

sections.h2: Starting a commercial foam project with us
sections.body:
Every commercial project starts with a paid inspection. We look at the roof surface, coating, foam or existing system, moisture, drainage, flashing and equipment, photograph what we find and give you a written estimate with our recommendation. Financing is available; ask during the estimate.

faqs: What information should a property manager have ready before a foam roof inspection?

Have the building address, roof access details, approximate roof size, any history of leaks with their locations and any records of past roof work or coatings. Contact information for whoever will meet us on site helps too. The more we know about the roof's history, the more useful the inspection is.
Who should be told before foam is sprayed on an occupied building?

Tenants, building staff and anyone who services rooftop equipment should know the schedule. Occupants near air intakes should expect some units to be turned off while we work nearby. Clear notice ahead of time prevents most complaints and surprises.
Can rooftop HVAC units stay in place during a foam roof project?

In most cases, yes. The foam and coating are applied around the curbs and supports rather than requiring units to be removed. Units near the work may need to be shut down for a while to keep odor and overspray out of the air intakes.
How does a foam roof affect a building's roof drains and scuppers?

Adding foam raises the roof surface, so drains and scuppers have to be detailed so water still flows into them without backing up. Done well, tapered foam can actually improve how water reaches them. This is planned during the design, not left for the crew to figure out on the roof.
Is a foam roof suitable for a restaurant with kitchen exhaust on the roof?

It can be, but grease and exhaust residue are hard on many coatings. The coating needs to be chosen for that exposure, and the area around the exhaust fan needs regular cleaning and inspection. Grease containment at the fan is also important.
Can foam be installed on a multi-family or HOA building?

Yes. Apartment, condo and HOA properties with low-slope or flat roofs often make good candidates. The main extra steps are coordinating with the board or management, giving residents notice and planning around shared air intakes and parking.
How do maintenance records help with a foam roof warranty?

Many warranties require documented inspections and maintenance to stay in force. Records of inspections, repairs and recoats show the roof has been cared for as required. They also help budget for the next recoat and answer questions if the building is sold.
Can a foam roof be part of a long-term capital plan?

Yes, and it fits well because the cycle is predictable: installation or restoration, regular inspections and repairs, then periodic recoats. Knowing roughly when each recoat is due lets owners spread costs over time instead of facing a sudden full replacement.
Should a commercial roof be checked for moisture before foam goes over it?

Always. Spraying foam or a restoration coating over wet insulation traps the moisture and leads to early failure. Moisture checks identify wet areas so they can be removed and replaced before the new system goes on.

faqCategory.title: Spray foam roofing and coatings
faqCategory.intro: Practical answers about spray polyurethane foam roofs, the coatings that protect them and how both hold up in the Arizona climate.
faqs: Why is only closed-cell foam used on roofs?

Closed-cell foam is dense and rigid, absorbs very little water and has the compressive strength to handle a roof surface. Open-cell foam is softer and more absorbent, which suits some interior insulation uses but not an exposed roof. Roofing-grade foam is made specifically for this job.
Can spray foam be applied to a roof with skylights?

Yes. Foam is sprayed up to and around the skylight curb, and the curb is flashed and coated like other penetrations. The skylight itself has to be protected from overspray during the work, and if the skylight is old or cracked, it makes sense to swap it out first.
How are scuppers handled when a foam roof is installed?

Scuppers are cleaned out, their flashing is checked or replaced and the foam is shaped so water flows into them instead of ponding in front of them. The coating is carried into the scupper opening and reinforced where needed. Since adding foam raises the roof surface, the scupper opening has to stay low enough to drain.
How does a foam roof tie into parapet walls?

Foam is typically carried up the parapet's inner wall, and sometimes over the top, so there's no open joint where the roof meets the wall. The coating covers it all as one surface. Cracked stucco or a failed parapet cap still has to be fixed, because water entering the wall from above can get behind the roof.
Can foam be shaped to steer water around a rooftop unit?

Yes. Foam can be built up into a small sloped ridge, called a cricket, on the high side of a unit or curb so water moves around it toward a drain. This is one of the ways foam handles drainage problems that are hard to fix with sheet roofing.
What happens to existing roof drains when foam is added?

Because foam raises the roof surface, the drain has to be detailed so water still runs into it, sometimes by adjusting or extending the drain or tapering the foam down to it. The drain is also cleaned and checked. A drain that ends up higher than the roof around it will leave water standing.
Does a thicker foam layer always mean a better roof?

Not by itself. More thickness adds insulation and can build slope, but the foam still has to bond well, be sprayed in proper passes and be fully coated. A well-applied roof at the specified thickness beats a thick layer installed poorly.
Can a foam roof be installed during the cooler winter months?

Often, yes. Foam and coatings have temperature and moisture limits set by the manufacturer, and winter mornings with dew or cold surfaces may shorten the working day. Dry, mild winter weather can actually be a good time for foam work in the Valley.
Why is foam not sprayed on windy days?

Wind carries fine overspray, which can land on cars, windows and neighboring buildings, and it can also affect how evenly the foam goes on. Crews watch wind conditions and stop or adjust when it picks up. That's one reason a foam schedule can shift by a day.
What are the signs that a roof coating went on too thin?

A coating applied too thin often wears through early, showing the foam texture or color within a few years. Thin areas may look uneven or chalk faster than the rest of the roof. Checking thickness during application is the best way to avoid it.
How can I protect my foam roof when a technician services my AC unit?

Ask technicians to use the walkway pads, avoid dragging tools or parts across the roof and not set sharp equipment or panels directly on the coating. If there are no walkway pads on the route to the unit, adding them is worth discussing. Any gouges or punctures should be repaired soon after.
What should I do if I notice a puncture in my foam roof?

Have it repaired soon, before water and UV can work into the foam. A small puncture is usually a quick fix: the damaged spot is cleaned, filled or sealed and recoated with compatible materials. Call us at 602-548-3770, and if we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.
Why shouldn't a foam roof be patched with whatever sealant is on hand?

Many sealants aren't compatible with foam or with the coating on the roof, especially silicone, and they can peel away or trap water. A mismatched patch can also make the next recoat harder. Repairs should use materials matched to the existing system.
Does a foam roof move as it heats up and cools down?

All roofs grow slightly in afternoon heat and shrink back at night. Roofing foam is dimensionally stable, and the elastomeric coating stretches and recovers with that daily movement. Structural joints in the building that move more than that need special detailing.
Can foam go over a roof that is currently leaking?

Only after the leak's source and any wet material are found and dealt with. An active leak usually means moisture inside the existing roof, and wet material has to be removed before foam goes on. Spraying over it would trap the water.
What is the difference between a primer and a base coat on a foam roof?

A primer is a thin layer that helps the next material bond to a surface, used where the substrate or product requires it. A base coat is the first full layer of the coating system, applied over the foam before the top coat. Not every system uses both.
How do evaporative cooler drips affect a foam roof?

Constant drips and overflow from a cooler keep one area of the roof wet and can leave mineral deposits, which wears the coating faster. Keeping the cooler's float and lines in good repair and directing its water to a drain helps. The area around the cooler deserves a close look at every inspection.
Can part of a foam roof be re-foamed while the rest is only recoated?

Yes. Areas with weathered, eroded or damaged foam can get new foam while sound areas are simply cleaned, repaired and recoated. The whole roof then gets a continuous coating so there are no weak transitions.
What causes cracks along the edges of a foam roof?

Edges see more movement and stress where the roof meets parapets, curbs and transitions, and coating there may also be thinner. Foot traffic and older flashing add to it. Edge cracks should be cleaned, repaired and recoated before water gets behind them.
How long should people stay off a roof after it is recoated?

Long enough for the coating to cure, which varies with the product, thickness, temperature and humidity. The crew will tell you when the roof can handle normal service traffic again. Keeping technicians off fresh coating avoids footprints and damage.
How soon after spraying does foam need to be coated?

Foam should be coated within the time window the manufacturer specifies, which is short, because UV starts affecting bare foam right away. Crews usually plan the work so foam and the base coat go on close together. Foam left uncoated too long may have to be prepared again before coating.
Can foam fix low spots on a flat patio cover?

Often, yes. Foam can be sprayed slightly thicker toward the high end so water runs off instead of sitting. The patio cover's framing has to be sound, and the joint where it meets the house needs careful flashing.
Should a foam roof be recoated before solar panels are installed?

When the coating is close to worn out, it's usually smart to recoat first, because recoating under panels later is harder and may require removing them. A roof with plenty of coating life left may only need an inspection and minor repairs before the installers start.
Can a home with a tile main roof have foam on its flat sections?

Yes, and many Valley homes do. The flat sections get foam and coating, while the tile roof keeps its own underlayment and flashing. The transition where the two meet needs careful work so water from the tile roof flows onto the foam instead of under it.
Why does a foam roof have a textured, orange-peel surface?

Spray foam naturally cures with a slightly bumpy texture, and roofers use it to judge application quality. A smooth to orange-peel texture is generally what you want, while very coarse or popcorn-like texture can trap water and be harder to coat. The coating follows the texture, so it's part of the finished look.
